title: Lusam / Lusum (Jericho)
summary: Lusam is a recorded older name for Jericho. Its inclusion on Indigenous place-name maps deserves context: Tooker questioned whether the name was Indigenous at all.
address_label: Present-day Jericho, NY — public orientation point at Jericho Public Library
map_geometry_source: Jericho association: Tooker 1911 p.86 and Jericho Public Library history. Modern public orientation point: OSM building 554784522; no historical parcel location asserted.
why_this_matters: Not every unfamiliar historical name is necessarily Indigenous. Keeping the evidence and the uncertainty together helps prevent an old attribution from becoming an unquestioned fact.
introduction_title: A Familiar Place, a Disputed Name
introduction_content: Lusam and Lusum are historical names associated with Jericho. Although nineteenth-century historian Benjamin F. Thompson described Lusam as an Indigenous name, Tooker questioned that attribution in 1911 and suggested it might instead be a shortened form of the English name Lewisham. That is a proposed explanation, not a proven origin.1
history_content:
Tooker cites a 1682 record of Indigenous people selling John Townsend fifty acres beside the cartway from Muskceta Cove to the farm called Lusam or Robert Williams’s plantation. He also cites a 1689 reference pairing Jericho and Lusam. These passages establish the name’s use in local records; they do not, by themselves, establish its language of origin.1

Jericho Public Library’s local history likewise associates Lusum with Jericho and describes a later change of name in 1692. Read alongside the earlier paired names reported by Tooker, this suggests caution about treating a single date as the first use of “Jericho.”2, 1
translation_title: What Can Be Said About the Name
translation_content: No Algonquian translation is asserted here. Lusam belongs in the story of how Long Island place names have been recorded and classified, including cases where an Indigenous attribution is disputed.1
whereintheworld_title: Location and Why the Pin Is Approximate
whereintheworld_content:
The historical identification is Jericho in the Town of Oyster Bay, supported by Tooker’s entry and the local library’s history. Neither source supplies a surveyed outline for Lusam or the fifty-acre parcel.1, 2

The pin uses Jericho Public Library at 1 Merry Lane as a present-day public point from which to explore this history. Its position follows the mapped library building. It does not claim that the library occupies the Indigenous transaction site, Robert Williams’s house or the center of an earlier settlement. The library maintains local books, maps, photographs and archival collections for further research.3, 2
